steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Criminal courts deal with offences against the state; civil courts deal with disputes between individuals or organisations

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: The Magistrates' Court hears 95% of criminal cases — summary offences and either-way offences

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: The Crown Court hears indictable offences (serious crimes) and appeals from the Magistrates' Court

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: The High Court hears the most serious civil cases, divided into three divisions: Queen's Bench, Chancery and Family

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Q: What is the difference between criminal and civil courts? | Q: What cases does the Crown Court hear? | Q: What are the three divisions of the High Court?

steps.title: Check your answers
steps.body: Criminal courts deal with offences against the state (prosecuted by the Crown); civil courts deal with disputes between individuals or organisations, where the claimant sues the defendant. | Indictable offences (serious crimes like murder and rape), either-way offences sent from the Magistrates' Court, and appeals from the Magistrates' Court against conviction or sentence. | Queen's Bench (contract and tort), Chancery (business, trusts, tax) and Family (divorce, children, financial remedies).

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Know the full court hierarchy for both criminal and civil cases Use the correct names: Magistrates' Court (not 'magistrate court'), Crown Court, High Court Explain the difference between summary, either-way and indictable offences Tribunals are increasingly important — know their advantages over courts ADR is often examined — know the three types and their benefits
